length.text: Males about 55-85 cm, females about 90-120 cm

overview.text: The Iberian Grass Snake, also called the Red-eyed Grass Snake, is the grass snake of Portugal, Spain, southern France and the coast of north-western Africa. For a long time it was treated as part of the common Grass Snake, but in 2016 scientists showed it is a separate species. It is not venomous to people and lives near water, where it hunts fish and frogs.

identification.text: Its most reliable feature is the reddish colour of the iris, which sets it apart from all other grass snakes. Compared with them it also has fewer belly scales and a differently shaped skull - details that need a specimen in the hand.

size.label: Adults
size.text: Females grow much larger than males: about 90-120 cm, against about 55-85 cm for males.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: The Iberian Peninsula (Portugal and Spain), neighbouring southern France, and scattered coastal areas of north-western Africa, in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. The snakes of Algeria and Tunisia are treated as a separate subspecies, *N. a. algerica*, and those of northern Morocco were described in 2025 as *N. a. soumiafahdae*. In North Africa it is rare and lives in small, separate patches.

habitat.text: Slow-flowing and still fresh water - streams, rivers, ponds and their banks - usually in the shallows. In Iberian rivers it is more numerous where there are no invasive fish.

diet.text: Mainly fish and amphibians; small mammals and young birds are also eaten.

reproduction.text: Lays eggs. Sources disagree on clutch size: young females are thought to lay around ten eggs, while large, older females may lay many more (figures of 50 and even 100 are given).

conservation.text: Sources disagree on its global status: one lists it as Least Concern in the European and global IUCN Red Lists, another as not yet evaluated. Andorra's national Red List rates it Vulnerable there.

taxonomy.text: Described by Seoane in the 1880s, then treated for over a century as a subspecies of the Grass Snake (*Natrix natrix astreptophora*). A 2016 study of its body shape, skull and DNA recognised it as a full species. Older field guides therefore call it a grass snake.
Fossils of this snake from Spain date from the late Pliocene to the late Pleistocene.

similar.text: shares its rivers in Iberia; the Viperine Snake is smaller and has a dark zigzag along its back and dark side spots, while the Iberian Grass Snake has reddish eyes.
the Barred Grass Snake, which meets it in France; it lacks the red iris.

names: *Natrix natrix astreptophora* (Seoane, 1884) - as a subspecies of the Grass Snake

funfacts.text: Scientists only recognised this snake as its own species in 2016 - it had been hiding in plain sight as a kind of grass snake.
